problem: The sentence says 'A limit in g/km or g/kWh is a mass per unit work.' Only g/kWh is mass per unit work. A g/km limit is mass per unit distance, so the sentence contradicts the definitions given just above it in the formula box.
fix: Write: 'A limit in g/km is a mass per unit distance; a limit in g/kWh is a mass per unit work.'

problem: The cycle is said to 'fix the work done'. For a g/km limit the cycle fixes the distance covered and the speed-time history; work only enters when the limit is in g/kWh. A student may think work is always measured for light vehicles.
fix: Say 'a fixed driving cycle that fixes the distance travelled and the speed-time history (and, for engine tests, the work done)' both in the lead and in the Q1 answer.

problem: The text jumps from 'up to BS-III, Indian cars were tested on the Indian Driving Cycle and its modified version' straight to BS-VI using WLTC. It leaves out BS-IV, which also used the Modified Indian Driving Cycle, so a reader cannot tell what was used between BS-III and BS-VI.
fix: Add: 'BS-IV cars continued on the Modified Indian Driving Cycle; BS-VI replaced it with the WLTC.'

where: Section 1 table, PM row for petrol car
problem: The table says PM is 'mostly not limited' for petrol cars. Under BS-VI a particle mass limit of 0.0045 g/km applies to petrol cars as well, so the entry is misleading for the standard the chapter is about.
fix: Change the petrol PM entry to 'limited under BS-VI at about 0.0045 g/km (5 thousandths of a g/km)' and keep 'not limited' only for older standards or say 'no PN limit'.

problem: The question tests a CO result against a 0.06 g/km limit. Real CO limits are of the order of 1 g/km; 0.06 g/km is a NOx-type number, so the numbers can plant a wrong memory of typical CO limits.
fix: Ask the student to compare 0.050 g/km CO with a 1.0 g/km CO limit, or change the pollutant to NOx if the 0.06 g/km limit is wanted.
